title: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
summary: Train a cheap student on a teacher's full output distribution: soft targets, temperature, the T-squared loss, a patient and consistent recipe, feature losses, sequence and on-policy LLM distillation, and when it fails.
outcomes: Explain why a teacher's soft targets carry more training signal than one-hot labels
Compute temperature-softened probabilities and the distillation loss for a small example
Explain why the soft loss is multiplied by T squared and what happens if you forget it
Set up a consistent, patient distillation run and judge it against a same-size supervised baseline
Match intermediate features with hints, attention maps or hidden-state losses, and say what alignment each needs
Choose between word-level, sequence-level and on-policy distillation for a language model
Plan an LLM distillation pipeline: top-k logit storage, tokenizer mismatch, reasoning traces, and whether to distill at all
Diagnose capacity-gap and fidelity failures and pick a fix such as a teacher assistant

lessons.title: Why a teacher's soft targets beat one-hot labels

blocks.md: Big models and ensembles (several independently trained models whose predictions are averaged) are usually the most accurate thing you can train. They are also the most expensive thing to serve: every request pays for all those parameters. Hinton, Vinyals and Dean (2015) put it with an insect analogy: a larva is built for feeding, the adult for travel, and there is no reason the model you train should be the model you deploy.

**Knowledge distillation** trains a small **student** network to imitate a large, already trained **teacher** (a single big model or an ensemble). The student learns from a **transfer set**, which can be the original training data or extra unlabeled inputs, and its targets come from the teacher's outputs instead of only the human labels. Afterwards you ship the student alone. The field abbreviates knowledge distillation as **KD**, as in Seq-KD and GKD later in this course.

The key move is what counts as knowledge. It is tempting to think of a model's knowledge as its weights, which makes it hard to see how a model of a different shape could hold the same thing. The paper's alternative view: the knowledge is the learned **mapping from inputs to outputs**, and a different network can be trained to reproduce that mapping.

blocks.title: The distillation pipeline

nodes.label:

+ true labels

scenes.caption: Step 1: train the teacher the normal way. It can be huge, heavily regularized, or an ensemble, because nobody has to serve it.
Step 2: freeze the teacher and run it on the transfer set. For every input it emits a whole probability distribution over classes, the soft targets.
Step 3: train the student on the same inputs so its outputs match the soft targets, usually mixed with a small loss on the true labels. Only the student's weights change.
Step 4: deploy the student alone. The teacher's cost was paid once, at training time.

blocks.md: Why should the teacher's outputs be better targets than the labels the teacher itself was trained on? Take an image classifier with five classes: cat, dog, fox, car, truck. The human label for a cat photo is **one-hot**: 1 for cat, 0 for everything else. A one-hot label is also called a **hard label**, because it allows no doubt. Recall that a classifier's last layer outputs **logits**, one raw score per class, and a softmax exponentiates them and divides by their total to get probabilities. A trained teacher instead says something like 89.8% cat, 7.4% dog, 2.7% fox, and well under 1% for the vehicles.

blocks.title: One-hot label versus the teacher's distribution (cat photo)

scenes.caption: The one-hot label: all mass on cat. It says nothing about which wrong answers are nearly right and which are absurd.
The teacher's output for the same photo (teacher logits 6, 3.5, 2.5, -1, -2 through a softmax): 89.8% cat, 7.37% dog, 2.71% fox, 0.08% car, 0.03% truck.

The wrong classes are not equally wrong. Dog is about 90 times more likely than car. This ranking of mistakes describes how the teacher generalizes, and it is information the one-hot label throws away.

blocks.md: Hinton et al. give a vivid version: a BMW may have a tiny chance of being mistaken for a garbage truck, but that mistake is still many times more likely than mistaking it for a carrot. Training on the full distribution teaches the student this **similarity structure**.

The paper's claim about information uses **entropy**, the standard measure of how spread out a distribution is: $H(p) = -\sum_i p_i \ln p_i$. Each term is a class's probability times its surprise, $-\ln p_i$, which is 0 for a certain event and grows as the event gets rarer, so $H$ is the average surprise. With the natural log the unit is the **nat** (natural unit of information). A one-hot label has entropy 0: it holds no doubt, so it tells you nothing beyond which class is right. A uniform distribution over 5 classes has the maximum, $\ln 5 = 1.609$ nats. Our cat teacher sits at 0.395 nats.

The paper notes two practical consequences: soft targets with high entropy carry much more information per example than a hard label, and their gradients vary less from example to example, so the student can often learn from less data and with a higher learning rate.

Why should the gradients vary less? Here is a two-example illustration of our own; the paper states the claim without numbers. Two cat photos: A is a clear cat, B looks a lot like a dog, and the teacher says B is 53.3% cat and 43.6% dog. Early in training the student gives A 82.6% cat and splits B evenly, 42.8% cat and 42.8% dog. The gradient on the student's logits is its probabilities minus the target: $q - y$ for a hard label, $q - p$ for soft targets at $T = 1$ (lesson 3 derives it).

With hard labels, B demands 100% cat and pushes its dog logit down by 0.428 while A barely touches dog, so the two examples pull in very different directions: their gradient vectors are 0.556 apart. With the teacher's targets both gradients are small and similar, only 0.048 apart, because the teacher already treats B as ambiguous.

blocks.title: Gradients for two cat photos: hard labels vs soft targets

scenes.caption: Hard label, gradient q - y. Photo B's gradient says: raise cat by a lot (-.572), push dog down hard (+.428). Photo A's says almost nothing about dog (+.041). The two updates disagree.
Soft targets from the teacher (logits 6, 3.5, 2.5, -1, -2 for A and 4, 3.8, 1, -1, -2 for B), gradient q - p. Both rows are now small and similar: the vectors are 0.048 apart instead of 0.556.

blocks.md: The paper's evidence comes from speech recognition. An **acoustic model** is the part of a recognizer that labels audio: Hinton et al.'s network reads a window of audio frames, each 10 ms apart, and classifies the current frame into one of 14,000 speech-sound states of a hidden Markov model (HMM), the statistical model that a decoder then uses to turn frame labels into words. **Frame accuracy** is the percentage of frames it labels correctly.

blocks.title: Evidence from Hinton et al.: speech acoustic model

scenes.caption: Test frame accuracy of an 85M-parameter speech model (Table 1). Ten models averaged reach 61.1% versus 58.9% for one.
A single model of the same size distilled from the ensemble reaches 60.8%, recovering (60.8 - 58.9) / (61.1 - 58.9), about 86% of the ensemble's gain, at one model's serving cost.

Table 5: trained on only 3% of the data with hard labels, the model overfits and early-stops at 44.5%. With soft targets from a model trained on all the data it reaches 57.0%, close to the full-data 58.9%, without early stopping.

blocks.md: The paper's MNIST experiment tells the same story with error counts. MNIST is a classic dataset of handwritten digits 0 to 9, small 28 by 28 grayscale images, with 60,000 for training and 10,000 for testing, so a test error count is out of 10,000. A big regularized net makes 67 test errors; a smaller net trained normally makes 146. The same small net trained to also match the big net's soft targets makes 74, closing most of the gap without seeing any new labeled data.

The teacher's knowledge is its input-to-output mapping, including how much probability it gives to each wrong answer. Distillation transfers that mapping by using the teacher's full output distribution as the training target.

Training the student on the teacher's top-1 prediction alone, its single most likely class (pseudo-labeling), is not the same thing in general (lesson 9 shows one setting where top-1 targets did well). It keeps the teacher's decision but discards the relative probabilities of the other classes, which is exactly the extra signal that makes distillation work.

blocks.question: In Hinton et al.'s speech experiment, a model trained with soft targets on 3% of the data nearly matched one trained on 100% with hard labels. What best explains this?
options: Each soft target carries information about every class, so one example teaches far more than a one-hot label
Soft targets contain the correct labels for the other 97% of the data
Soft targets remove the need for a loss function on the student
The student had more parameters than the teacher
blocks.explain: A one-hot label says only which class is right. A soft target also says how plausible each wrong class is, which encodes what the teacher learned from the full dataset. That extra information per example, plus lower-variance gradients, acts as a strong regularizer, so the small subset goes much further.

blocks.question: A colleague says distillation is pointless if the student has the same architecture as one member of the ensemble teacher, because that architecture was already trained on the data. Based on the speech result, what is the best reply?
options: They are right: the distilled model can never beat a normally trained model of the same size
Only the ensemble matters, so the student should be deleted
The distilled single model recovered most of the ensemble's improvement, so the same architecture trained on soft targets beats the same architecture trained on labels
Distillation only helps when the student is larger than the teacher
blocks.explain: Table 1 of Hinton et al.: same architecture, same data, but trained on ensemble soft targets it reached 60.8% frame accuracy versus 58.9% with hard labels. The training targets, not just the architecture, determine what the network learns.

blocks.md: There is a catch. A good teacher is very confident on most training examples. On MNIST, Hinton et al. describe one image of a 2 getting probability $10^{-6}$ of being a 3 and $10^{-9}$ of being a 7, while another 2 has these reversed. That ratio is exactly the similarity information we want, but probabilities that close to zero barely change a cross-entropy loss, so the student would hardly learn from them.

The fix is a **temperature** $T$ in the softmax. Recall that a softmax turns **logits** (the raw scores $z_i$ before the softmax) into probabilities. Dividing every logit by $T$ before exponentiating gives:

blocks.caption: Hinton et al. Eq. 1. T = 1 is the ordinary softmax; T greater than 1 gives a softer distribution.

blocks.md: Why does this soften the distribution without destroying it? The ratio of two probabilities is $q_i / q_j = \exp((z_i - z_j)/T)$. Dividing by $T$ shrinks every logit gap by the same factor, so the ranking of classes never changes, but large ratios get compressed. For our cat teacher the dog and car logits differ by 4.5, so dog is $e^{4.5} \approx 90$ times more likely than car at $T=1$, but only $e^{4.5/4} \approx 3.08$ times at $T=4$. Now car carries enough mass to matter in the loss.

blocks.title: The same teacher logits at rising temperature

scenes.caption: T = 1: 89.8% on cat. The vehicles get 0.08% and 0.03%, too small to influence training.
T = 2: logit gaps are halved. Cat drops to 66.28%, dog rises to 18.99%, car to 2.0%.
T = 4: a clearly informative distribution (44.22, 23.67, 18.44, 7.68, 5.99). The ranking is unchanged; only the contrast is lower.
T = 8: entropy is 1.545 nats against a maximum of ln 5 = 1.609 for a uniform distribution. The differences are getting small.
T = 20: nearly uniform (24.41% to 16.36%). The information is still there, but only in small deviations from 20% each.

blocks.title: Each class's probability as temperature rises

scenes.caption: The top class: cat falls from 0.90 at T = 1 toward 0.2 (one fifth) as T grows.
The runner-up classes dog and fox first rise, then also flatten toward 0.2. They never cross cat: temperature never reorders classes.
The near-zero classes car and truck rise the most in relative terms. Somewhere around T = 2 to 5 every class carries visible mass while the ranking is still sharp.

blocks.md: In distillation the teacher produces its soft targets at a high temperature, and the student is trained with **the same** temperature in its own softmax so the two distributions are comparable. After training the student runs at $T = 1$ like any other model. The same convention appears in DistilBERT, a distilled version of the BERT language model that lesson 9 covers: the temperature is shared by teacher and student during training and set back to 1 at inference.

blocks.prompt: Push T toward infinity. Both teacher and student distributions approach uniform (20% each). Does the distillation signal vanish, or does it turn into something else?
blocks.reveal: It turns into **logit matching**. Hinton et al. show that for $T$ much larger than the logits, and with each example's logits shifted to mean zero, the gradient becomes proportional to $z_i - v_i$, where $z_i$ is the student's logit and $v_i$ the teacher's for the same class. That is exactly the gradient of a squared error between the two logit vectors, the logit-matching method of Caruana and colleagues, so it is a special case of distillation. Lesson 3 derives it.

blocks.md: Which temperature should you pick? It trades two things. Higher $T$ pays more attention to the very negative logits (the classes the teacher considers nearly impossible), which may carry useful knowledge but are also nearly unconstrained by the teacher's own training and therefore noisy. Hinton et al. found that on MNIST, with 300 or more units per layer in the student, all temperatures above 8 gave fairly similar results, but with only 30 units per layer, temperatures of 2.5 to 4 worked significantly better. Small students do best when they can ignore the noisiest part of the teacher. Cho and Hariharan (2019) report that popular choices in prior work are $T \in \{3, 4, 5\}$.

Temperature does not change the argmax, the class with the highest score. Running the deployed student at T greater than 1 does not change its top-1 predictions at all; it only makes its probabilities less confident. Temperature is a training-time device for distillation (and a separate sampling knob for generative models).

Tune T like any hyperparameter on held-out data. It is not universal: Kim and Rush tested T in 1, 1.5 and 2 for word-level distillation of translation models (token-by-token distillation, lesson 6) and found T = 1 worked best.

blocks.question: At T = 1 the teacher thinks dog is 90 times more likely than car (logit gap 4.5). What is that ratio at T = 4?
options: 90, temperature preserves ratios
About 3.08, because the ratio is exp(4.5 / 4)
22.5, the ratio divides by T
1, every class becomes equally likely
blocks.explain: The probability ratio is exp of the logit gap divided by T: exp(4.5 / 4) = exp(1.125), about 3.08. Temperature divides the logit gap, so the probability ratio shrinks exponentially, not linearly. The ordering is preserved; the ratio is not.

blocks.question: You distill a large image classifier into a very small student with 30 units per layer. Following Hinton et al.'s MNIST findings, which temperature range is the best starting point?
options: T = 1, since small students need sharp targets
T = 20 or more, to transfer every logit
Temperature has no effect on small students
An intermediate T around 2.5 to 4
blocks.explain: With 30 units per layer, temperatures of 2.5 to 4 worked significantly better than higher or lower ones. A tiny student cannot absorb all the teacher's knowledge; an intermediate T lets it ignore the very negative, noisy logits while still learning the runner-up structure.

lessons.title: The distillation loss and why it is scaled by T squared

blocks.md: Now the precise recipe. Let $v_i$ be the teacher's logits and $z_i$ the student's. Write $p^{(T)}$ for the teacher's softmax at temperature $T$ and $q^{(T)}$ for the student's. When true labels $y$ are available, Hinton et al. found it best to take a weighted average of two objectives: a soft one that matches the teacher at temperature $T$, and a hard one that is ordinary cross-entropy with the labels at $T = 1$, given considerably lower weight. The weight on the soft term is called $\alpha$, between 0 and 1, and the hard term gets $1 - \alpha$.

The soft term measures the mismatch with the **Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence**, named after Solomon Kullback and Richard Leibler (1951): $\mathrm{KL}(p \| q) = \sum_i p_i \ln(p_i / q_i)$. It comes from cross-entropy. If outcomes follow $p$ but you score them with $q$, your average loss is the cross-entropy: for each class, its probability $p_i$ times its loss $-\ln q_i$, summed. The best you can do is score them with $p$ itself, which gives the entropy $H(p)$ from the first lesson. KL is the gap between the two: cross-entropy minus entropy weights each class's difference $\ln p_i - \ln q_i$ by $p_i$, and the two logs combine into $\sum_i p_i \ln(p_i / q_i)$. So KL is the extra nats you pay for using $q$ instead of $p$. It is never negative, it is 0 only when $q = p$, and it is not symmetric: $\mathrm{KL}(p \| q)$ and $\mathrm{KL}(q \| p)$ differ, which lesson 7 puts to use.

blocks.caption: In words: alpha times T squared times the KL divergence from the teacher's softened distribution to the student's, plus one minus alpha times the usual cross-entropy with the true label y. Both terms use the same student logits z; only the temperature differs.

blocks.md: The paper writes the soft term as cross-entropy with the soft targets; using KL divergence instead gives the same gradients. That is the gap just derived, rearranged: cross-entropy equals the teacher's entropy plus the KL divergence, $\mathrm{CE}(p, q) = H(p) + \mathrm{KL}(p \| q)$, and $H(p)$ does not depend on the student. For our cat example at $T = 4$: $H(p) = 1.379$, KL $= 0.048$, cross-entropy $= 1.427$. KL is convenient because it is 0 when the student matches perfectly.

The gradient of the soft cross-entropy with respect to a student logit is short and tells you everything. To see where it comes from, write the soft loss as $C = -\sum_j p_j \ln q_j$ with $\ln q_j = z_j/T - \ln \sum_k \exp(z_k/T)$. Differentiate with respect to $z_i$. The first piece only touches term $j = i$ and gives $-p_i/T$. The log of the sum has derivative $q_i/T$; it appears in every term, weighted by $p_j$, and the $p_j$ add up to 1, so it gives $+q_i/T$. Adding the two pieces gives Hinton et al.'s equation 2:

blocks.caption: Hinton et al. Eq. 2: the student's softened probability minus the teacher's, divided by T.

blocks.md:
Two factors shrink this as $T$ grows. One $1/T$ is explicit, from the chain rule through $z_i/T$. The other is hidden in $q_i - p_i$: at high temperature both distributions approach uniform, so their difference shrinks roughly like $1/T$ too.

To make that exact, use $\exp(x) \approx 1 + x$, which holds when $x = z_i/T$ is small, that is, when $T$ is large. With $N$ classes, the softmax numerator becomes $1 + z_i/T$ and the denominator becomes $N$ plus the sum of all the $z_j/T$. If each example's logits are shifted to mean zero, that sum is 0, so $q_i \approx 1/N + z_i/(NT)$, and the same for the teacher, $p_i \approx 1/N + v_i/(NT)$. Subtracting cancels the $1/N$ and leaves $(z_i - v_i)/(NT)$. Times the explicit $1/T$, that is Hinton et al.'s equation 4:

blocks.caption: N is the number of classes. This is the gradient of a squared error between student and teacher logits, so in the high-temperature limit distillation is logit matching, and the gradient scale falls like 1 over T squared.

blocks.md: That $1/T^2$ is why the soft loss is multiplied by $T^2$. Without it, raising $T$ from 2 to 8 would silently cut the soft term's gradients by up to 16 times relative to the hard-label term, because $(8/2)^2 = 16$ (exactly 16 only in the high-temperature limit; in the worked example below the drop is about 9 times, since T = 2 is not yet in that regime), so changing the temperature would also change the effective mixing weight. With the factor, in the paper's words, the relative contributions of hard and soft targets stay roughly unchanged as you vary $T$.

scenes.caption: Soft-target gradient at T = 1, (q - p) / T. Negative means gradient descent raises that logit. The student under-rates cat and dog and over-rates fox.
Compare the hard-label gradient (q - onehot) at T = 1. It pushes dog DOWN (+.041) because dog is wrong. The teacher's soft target pushed dog UP. Labels and teacher disagree about how wrong dog is.

scenes.caption: Length of the unscaled gradient vector: 0.1167 at T = 1 down to 0.0016 at T = 20, a drop of about 70 times. The soft term fades away.
Multiplied by T squared the length levels off near 0.6397, approaching the logit-matching limit of 0.6542. Now T controls what is matched, not how loud it is.

blocks.title: Computing the loss for one example
blocks.code:
T, alpha = 4.0, 0.9
v = [6.0, 3.5, 2.5, -1.0, -2.0]  # teacher logits
z = [4.0, 1.0, 2.0, 0.0, -1.0]   # student logits
label = 0                        # true class: cat
p = softmax([a / T for a in v])  # soft targets
q = softmax([a / T for a in z])  # student at T
kl = sum(pi * log(pi / qi) for pi, qi in zip(p, q))
soft = T * T * kl
hard = -log(softmax(z)[label])   # T = 1
loss = alpha * soft + (1 - alpha) * hard

scenes.caption: Setup: temperature 4, soft weight 0.9, the same teacher and student logits as above, true class cat.
Soft targets and the student's softened distribution, both at T = 4.
KL divergence from teacher to student, then the T squared factor (16).
Hard-label cross-entropy at T = 1. The student already gives cat 82.6%, so this term is small.
Weighted sum. The soft term dominates, as Hinton et al. recommend.

blocks.code:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def distill_loss(student_logits, teacher_logits, labels, T=4.0, alpha=0.9):
    # Soft part: KL(teacher_T || student_T), scaled by T*T (Hinton et al.)
    log_q = F.log_softmax(student_logits / T, dim=-1)
    log_p = F.log_softmax(teacher_logits / T, dim=-1)
    soft = F.kl_div(log_q, log_p, log_target=True, reduction="batchmean") * T * T
    # Hard part: ordinary cross-entropy on the true labels at T = 1
    hard = F.cross_entropy(student_logits, labels)
    return alpha * soft + (1 - alpha) * hard

# in the training loop
teacher.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    teacher_logits = teacher(x)   # the teacher is frozen
loss = distill_loss(student(x), teacher_logits, y)
loss.backward()
blocks.caption: PyTorch version. F.kl_div takes the student's log-probabilities first and the target second; batchmean sums the KL over classes and divides by the number of examples, which matches the math definition. The official PyTorch tutorial writes the same loss by hand.

blocks.md: Classic bugs: (1) forgetting the T squared factor, so changing T quietly reweights the losses; (2) using `reduction="mean"` in `kl_div`, which divides by batch size times number of classes, not batch size (the [PyTorch docs](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.KLDivLoss.html) warn about this); (3) swapping the arguments; (4) letting gradients flow into the teacher or leaving it in training mode (dropout on, batch statistics in batch normalization).

How should you set $\alpha$? There is no universal value. Hinton et al. found the best results with a considerably lower weight on the hard term, as above, while the PyTorch tutorial's example goes the other way: 0.25 on the soft term and 0.75 on the label term with $T = 2$, for a short 10-epoch run. Two cases are clear-cut. With an unlabeled transfer set there is no hard term at all, so $\alpha = 1$: **pure distillation**. Beyer et al. (next lesson) use the KL term alone even when labels exist, and so does a large study of language-model distillation (Busbridge et al., lesson 8).

Because $T$ changes how far the soft targets sit from one-hot labels, tune $T$ and $\alpha$ together on held-out data rather than one after the other. Beyer et al. sweep $T \in \{1, 2, 5, 10\}$ jointly with learning rate and weight decay for every setting they compare.
Soft gradient = (q - p) / T, which shrinks like 1 over T squared. Multiply the soft loss by T squared so temperature changes what is matched without changing how much it counts.

blocks.question: Your loss uses F.kl_div(log_q, log_p, log_target=True, reduction="mean") on a batch of 32 examples over 1000 classes, then multiplies by T squared. Compared with the intended loss, the soft term is:
options: 1000 times too small, because mean divides by every element, not by the batch size
Correct as written
32 times too large
Equal to the cross-entropy instead of KL
blocks.explain: With reduction="mean" PyTorch averages over all 32 x 1000 elements. The KL per example is a sum over classes, so the mathematically correct reduction is batchmean (sum divided by 32). The soft term ends up 1000 times smaller and the hard loss silently dominates.

blocks.question: You raise T from 2 to 8 but your code has no T squared factor. Keeping alpha fixed, what happens to training?
options: Nothing, temperature only affects the soft targets' shape
The student learns the teacher more aggressively
The soft term's gradients shrink by roughly 16 times, so training becomes mostly hard-label training
The hard-label term disappears
blocks.explain: The soft gradient scales roughly as 1 over T squared, and (8/2) squared = 16. Without the compensating factor, the effective weight of the teacher drops sharply and your experiment is really testing a different mixing weight.

blocks.question: Your transfer set is 2 million unlabeled product photos plus 5,000 labeled ones. What is a sensible way to set alpha?
options: alpha = 0, since human labels are more reliable than any teacher
alpha = 0.5 everywhere, so neither term dominates
Copy the PyTorch tutorial's 0.25 soft and 0.75 hard weights
alpha = 1 (pure distillation) on the unlabeled photos, and tune alpha jointly with T on held-out data for the labeled ones
blocks.explain: Unlabeled examples have no hard-label term, so only the soft loss applies to them. Where labels exist, the right mix is an empirical question: Hinton et al. found a low hard-label weight best, the tutorial uses the opposite, and T shifts the balance, so tune T and alpha together on held-out data.

lessons.title: A patient and consistent teacher: the recipe that makes KD work

blocks.md:
You now have the loss. The obvious way to use it: run the teacher once over your 1,020 training photos, save its logits to disk, then train the student on those saved targets for a common 100 epochs while applying random crops to its inputs. It is cheap and it feels correct.

Beyer et al. (2021) show that both habits, caching the teacher's outputs and stopping at a normal schedule, are exactly what make distillation look weak. Their paper, *Knowledge distillation: A good teacher is patient and consistent*, compresses a large ResNet (BiT-ResNet-152x2, a 152-layer ResNet twice as wide from Google's Big Transfer models, about 10 times the compute of a ResNet-50) into a ResNet-50 and finds that the recipe matters as much as the loss.

Their key move is a change of view. Distillation is not "training on better labels"; it is **function matching**: the student should compute the same function as the teacher, and every input where you ask both of them is one more point where the two functions must agree.

That view makes two rules obvious. First, be **consistent**: teacher and student must see the exact same input, including the same random crop and the same noise, or the target describes a different picture than the one the student sees. Second, be **patient**: matching a function on many points takes far longer than fitting one label per image. A third ingredient widens the set of points: **mixup**, which blends two images pixel by pixel into a new input, here with an aggressive mixing weight drawn uniformly from 0 to 1. A blend of a cat and a car has no true label, but the teacher still has an answer, so it is a valid point to match on.

blocks.title: Four ways to feed teacher and student (Beyer et al., Figure 2)

scenes.caption: Fixed teacher: the teacher's output for one fixed view is computed once and cached. The student sees a fresh random crop each step, so its target often describes a different picture.
Independent noise: the teacher runs live, but on its own random crop. Teacher and student still answer about different inputs.
Consistent teaching: crop once and feed the same view to both. Now the target is the teacher's answer for exactly what the student sees.
Function matching: consistent teaching plus aggressive mixup, so the shared view can be a blend of two images. More distinct points on which the two functions must agree.

blocks.md:
The ImageNet numbers (Table 3 of the paper, ResNet-50 student, teacher at 83.0% top-1) show both rules at once. With a fixed teacher, the student peaks at 78.11% after 1,200 epochs and then gets worse (76.95% at 9,600): it overfits the cached targets. Consistent teaching keeps improving to 81.76%, and function matching reaches 82.31%, 0.69 points short of the teacher. For comparison, the paper's best ResNet-50 trained on labels alone with the same setup reaches 78.15%.

The schedule matters as much as the setup. At 30 epochs, function matching (73.89%) is slightly *behind* plain consistent teaching (74.95%): mixup makes the task harder, and a short run underfits it. The authors warn that choices that look worse at normal length often end up best for long runs, and the reverse.

blocks.title: ImageNet: points below the teacher (83.0%), lower is better

scenes.caption: 30 epochs: all three are 8 to 9 points behind. Consistent teaching leads (gap 8.05); function matching (9.11) is no better than the fixed teacher (9.25) yet.
300 epochs: the consistent setups pull away (2.92 and 2.70) while the fixed teacher stalls at 5.24.
1,200 epochs: function matching is 1.46 behind, consistent teaching 1.85, fixed teacher 4.89, its best result.
9,600 epochs: the fixed teacher has overfit and slipped back to 6.05. Function matching is 0.69 points from the teacher. Patience pays only when the teacher is consistent.

blocks.md: How long is patient? On the small Pets dataset (3,312 training images), the paper's ResNet-50 student reaches 82.75% after 300 epochs, 90.08% after 3,000 and 91.06% after 30,000, matching the 91.03% teacher. A ResNet-50 trained from scratch on the labels gets 74.24%, and one transferred from ImageNet-21k pretraining gets 88.20%. The paper's own summary: the teacher is always reached eventually, after far more epochs than anyone would use for supervised training, and on these datasets they saw no overfitting even at a million epochs on Flowers102. A common 100-epoch run lands well below the transfer baseline.

blocks.prompt: You have a fixed compute budget of about 30 ImageNet epochs. Should you turn on aggressive mixup (function matching) or just feed consistent crops?
blocks.reveal: Plain consistent teaching. In Table 3 of Beyer et al. it leads at 30 epochs (74.95% vs 73.89%). Function matching only wins once the schedule is long (from 300 epochs on), because the blended inputs are harder to fit. A recipe that wins at 9,600 epochs can lose at 30, so test it at the length you will actually run.

blocks.md:
Which inputs should the transfer set contain? Beyer et al. test this directly. **In-domain** images (the task's own training images) work best. Images that are **related or overlapping** (ImageNet photos used to distill a Pets model) can come close but may need an extra long schedule. Even **unrelated** images work to some extent: a student that only ever saw Food101 photos, softly labeled by the teacher as pet breeds, learned to classify pets with roughly 30% accuracy. Labels are optional: their loss is the teacher-student KL alone, with no hard-label term.

Measure a run in two ways. **Generalization**: test accuracy of the student against a same-size model trained on labels (from scratch and, if you have one, a pretrained-and-fine-tuned baseline), since that is what distillation has to beat. **Fidelity**: how well the student copies the teacher, for example **top-1 agreement**, the fraction of test inputs where the two pick the same class, as defined by Stanton et al. (lesson 9).

blocks.code:
def train_student(mode, epochs, T=2.0):
    s = mlp(32); opt = torch.optim.Adam(s.parameters(), 1e-3)
    with torch.no_grad():
        cached = teacher(Xs)             # BUG: once, on unaugmented images
    for ep in range(epochs):
        perm = torch.randperm(len(Xs))
        for i in range(0, len(Xs), 64):
            idx = perm[i:i + 64]
            x = augment(Xs[idx])         # random shift + mixup, new every step
            if mode == "fixed":
                t = cached[idx]          # target describes a different input
            else:
                with torch.no_grad():
                    t = teacher(x)       # FIX: the same view the student sees
            loss = F.kl_div(F.log_softmax(s(x) / T, -1),
                            F.log_softmax(t / T, -1),
                            log_target=True, reduction="batchmean") * T * T
            opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    return s
blocks.caption: The core of a small experiment we ran on a laptop CPU: synthetic 10-class 12 by 12 images, a 512-wide MLP teacher trained on 10,000 images, a 32-wide MLP student distilled on a transfer set of 200 images. The only difference between the two modes is where the teacher's target comes from.

blocks.md: We ran it with three seeds per setting and also trained the same 32-wide student on the 200 labels alone (shift augmentation, cross-entropy) as the supervised baseline. The teacher scores 93.7% on 5,000 test images. The pattern of the paper shows up even at this toy scale: the fixed teacher peaks and then declines, and the consistent teacher keeps climbing. The consistent student beats the supervised baseline from 100 epochs on; the fixed one is far behind it at 100 epochs and passes it only on long runs, by less (82.2% vs 79.5% at 1,000 epochs). Top-1 agreement with the teacher after 3,000 epochs is 91.7% for the consistent student and 82.7% for the fixed one.

blocks.title: Our toy run: student test accuracy (mean of 3 seeds)

scenes.caption: 10 epochs (40 updates): nothing has been learned yet. Fixed 17.0%, consistent 20.4%, labels only 22.1%.
100 epochs: the consistent student (81.5%) passes the labels-only baseline (79.8%); the fixed teacher's student lags at 65.9%.
1,000 epochs: consistent 88.2%, fixed 82.2%, labels only 79.5% and already overfitting.
3,000 epochs: the fixed teacher's student has slipped to 81.0% while the consistent one is still rising (88.7%). Same direction as the ImageNet table, at toy scale.

blocks.md: Caching teacher outputs is only safe when the student's input is exactly the cached input. With random crops, flips, noise or mixup on the student side, cache the augmentation too or run the teacher live on the same batch. For language models the input is the token sequence itself, so the same rule says: teacher and student must score the same tokens.

Treat distillation as function matching: same input to teacher and student every step, as many distinct inputs as you can generate, and a schedule far longer than supervised training. Judge the run against a same-size model trained on labels, and track agreement with the teacher.

blocks.question: Two runs differ only in schedule: 30 epochs and 9,600 epochs. Following Beyer et al.'s ImageNet table, which setup should win each run?
options: Function matching wins both; mixup always helps
Consistent teaching wins the short run; function matching wins the long run
The fixed teacher wins the short run, because caching is cheaper per step
All three tie at 9,600 epochs because every student eventually matches the teacher
blocks.explain: At 30 epochs consistent teaching leads (74.95% vs 73.89% for function matching). At 9,600 epochs function matching is best (82.31%), consistent teaching close behind (81.76%), and the fixed teacher has overfit (76.95%). Mixup only pays off when there is time to fit the harder inputs.

blocks.question: A colleague's distillation loop computes teacher logits once per epoch on the unaugmented images and applies random crops plus mixup to the student's inputs. Training loss drops fast but test accuracy stalls below a labels-only baseline. What is the most direct fix?
options: Raise the temperature so the cached targets are softer
Lower the learning rate so the student fits the cached targets more slowly
Remove augmentation from the student so the cached targets fit
Run the teacher on the same augmented batch the student sees, every step
blocks.explain: The targets describe different inputs than the student sees, which is the fixed-teacher setup that overfits in Beyer et al. Removing augmentation would make the targets consistent but throws away the extra points that make long training useful. Feeding the same augmented view to both keeps the augmentation and makes the target correct.

lessons.title: Matching what the teacher computes inside: hints, attention, states

blocks.md:
For a cat photo the teacher's output is five probabilities. Halfway through the network, the same teacher has computed thousands of numbers about that photo: which regions look like fur, where the edges are. Output distillation shows the student only the final five. **Feature distillation** adds losses that make some of the student's intermediate activations match the teacher's, so the student also gets told how to get there.

The catch shows up immediately: a smaller student has smaller layers. A teacher layer with 32 channels cannot be compared number by number with a student layer that has 16. Each method in this lesson is a different answer to that mismatch.

**FitNets** (Romero et al., 2014) trained students that are thinner *and deeper* than their teachers, which were hard to train at the time. A **hint** is the output of a teacher hidden layer; the student's **guided layer** learns to predict it. Both are chosen in the middle of their networks, because hinting a deep student layer over-regularizes it.

Since the teacher is wider, a small **regressor** $r$ with its own weights $W_r$ sits on top of the guided layer and maps it to the hint's size. Training has two stages. Stage 1 trains the student up to the guided layer, plus the regressor, to minimize the squared error to the hint. Stage 2 throws the regressor away and trains the whole student with the ordinary distillation loss of lesson 3.

blocks.tex: \mathcal{L}_{HT}(W_{\mathrm{Guided}}, W_r) = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\big\| u_h(x; W_{\mathrm{Hint}}) - r\big(v_g(x; W_{\mathrm{Guided}}); W_r\big) \big\|^2
blocks.caption: FitNets Eq. 3. u_h is the teacher up to its hint layer, v_g the student up to its guided layer, r the regressor. The paper notes u_h and r must use the same nonlinearity so their outputs are comparable.

blocks.title: FitNets: hint training, then distillation

nodes.label:
Rest of student
and its output

Stage 2: KD loss
on soft targets

scenes.caption: Stage 1: the frozen teacher produces the hint. The student's first g layers plus the regressor are trained so that r(guided) matches the hint. Nothing above the guided layer is trained yet.
Stage 2: starting from those weights, the whole student is trained with the soft-target loss. The regressor was only scaffolding and is discarded.

blocks.md:
How big must the regressor be? If the guided and hint layers are convolutional, a fully connected regressor needs one weight per pair of input and output numbers. Take the shapes from the PyTorch distillation tutorial: student feature map 16 channels by 8 by 8, teacher 32 by 8 by 8. Fully connected, that is $(16 \cdot 64) \times (32 \cdot 64) = 2{,}097{,}152$ weights. FitNets instead uses a convolutional regressor, and the tutorial's version is a 3 by 3 convolution from 16 to 32 channels: $3 \cdot 3 \cdot 16 \cdot 32 = 4{,}608$ weights plus 32 biases.

On CIFAR-10, the paper's FitNet with about 2.5M parameters reached 91.61% test accuracy, above its 9M-parameter teacher at 90.18%. The authors also tried giving the middle layer a hint from the labels instead of the teacher; that thin, deep network failed to learn, and they suggest the teacher's hint works because it is a smoother target than the labels.

**Attention transfer** (Zagoruyko and Komodakis, 2017) avoids the regressor altogether. Take a convolutional layer's activation tensor $A$ with $C$ channels, each an $H \times W$ grid. Square every activation and sum over channels: $F(A) = \sum_{c=1}^{C} A_c^2$. The result is a single $H \times W$ map of where the layer is most active, the paper's **spatial attention map**. The channel count has been summed away, so a 32-channel teacher and a 16-channel student produce maps of the same shape as long as their grids match (otherwise one map can be interpolated to the other's size).

Each map is flattened into a vector $Q$ and divided by its length, then the loss penalizes the distance between student and teacher vectors, summed over the chosen layer pairs. The normalization matters, the authors stress: it compares where the layers look, not how large their activations are.

blocks.caption: Attention transfer, Eq. 2 of the paper: the usual cross-entropy plus beta over 2 times the distance between normalized attention maps for each chosen pair j. The paper sets beta so that it is about 0.1 in practice.

blocks.title: Attention maps on a 3 by 3 grid (normalized)

scenes.caption: Teacher: 4 channels of 3 by 3 activations, squared and summed over channels, gives the map 1, 1, 0 / 1, 18, 6 / 0, 2, 0. Divided by its length (19.16) it becomes these numbers: the teacher looks at the center and a bit to the right.

A student with only 2 channels gives the map 1, 2, 0 / 2, 5, 1 / 0, 0, 1 (length 6.0). Its attention leaks to the top-left and the bottom-right corner. Distance to the teacher's normalized map: 0.493.
A better-matched 2-channel student, with map 0, 1, 0 / 1, 13, 5 / 0, 2, 0 is only 0.083 away. Different widths, same shape of attention, and no regressor needed.

blocks.md: On CIFAR-10 with wide residual networks (WRN-16-2 teacher at 6.31% error, a half-width WRN-16-1 student at 8.77%), attention transfer cut the student's error to 7.93%. In the same table, transferring the full activations through 1 by 1 convolution regressors, FitNets style, only reached 8.51%, and plain output distillation reached 7.41%. Combining the two methods does not always add up: AT plus KD gave 7.51% for this pair, though it was the best of the four methods for the other three pairs in the table. Feature losses are a complement to the output loss, not a replacement.

Transformers offer more to match. **BERT** (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers, Devlin et al., 2018) is a Transformer encoder pretrained by **masked language modeling**: hide some input tokens and predict them from the words on both sides. BERT-base has 12 layers with 768-wide hidden states.

**TinyBERT** (Jiao et al., 2019) distills it into 4 layers that are only 312 wide. A mapping function $n = g(m)$ says which teacher layer student layer $m$ learns from; TinyBERT uses $g(m) = 3m$, so student layers 1 to 4 learn from teacher layers 3, 6, 9 and 12. Layer 0 is the embedding layer and the prediction layer is matched to the teacher's prediction layer. Each Transformer layer gets two losses: the mean squared error between **attention matrices** (each head scores how much every token draws on every other, a sequence-length square grid), averaged over heads and taken before the softmax, which converged faster, and the squared error between hidden states, after a learned $W_h$ maps the 312-wide student state to 768 wide.

blocks.tex: \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{layer}} = \begin{cases} \mathrm{MSE}(E^S W_e, E^T) & m = 0 \\ \mathrm{MSE}(H^S W_h, H^T) + \frac{1}{h}\sum_{i=1}^{h} \mathrm{MSE}(A_i^S, A_i^T) & 0 < m \le M \\ \mathrm{CE}(z^T / t,\, z^S / t) & m = M + 1 \end{cases}
blocks.caption: TinyBERT's loss for student layer m, matched to teacher layer g(m): embeddings, then attention matrices A for each of h heads plus hidden states H, then soft cross-entropy on the logits z with temperature t (t = 1 worked well).

blocks.title: TinyBERT's layer mapping g(m) = 3m

scenes.caption: Embedding layer: the 312-wide student embeddings are mapped by a learned W_e and compared with the teacher's by squared error.
Transformer layers: student layer m learns from teacher layer 3m, so the student sees the teacher's whole depth. Each pair compares attention matrices head by head and hidden states through W_h.
Prediction layer: ordinary soft-target distillation on the logits, used in the task-specific stage.

The paper's ablation tried learning only from the top four teacher layers (9 to 12) or the bottom four (1 to 4). The uniform mapping beat both on every task tested; which layers matter depends on the task.

blocks.md: TinyBERT runs this in two stages: **general distillation** from pretrained BERT on English Wikipedia text (no prediction-layer loss), then **task-specific distillation** from a fine-tuned BERT on that task's data, expanded with word-replacement augmentation. The reported result: TinyBERT4 keeps more than 96.8% of BERT-base's performance on GLUE, a benchmark of nine English language-understanding tasks (lesson 9 uses it again), while being 7.5 times smaller and 9.4 times faster at inference.

**DistilBERT** (lesson 9 covers its full recipe) takes the simplest route: its student keeps BERT's 768-wide hidden states, so no projection is needed. Its paper only says a cosine embedding loss "will tend to align the directions" of the student and teacher hidden-state vectors. The training code ([distiller.py](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers-research-projects/blob/main/distillation/distiller.py)) shows which states are paired: the **last layer** of the student and the last layer of the teacher, at every token position that is not padding. PyTorch's `CosineEmbeddingLoss` with target 1 is $1 - \cos$, averaged over those positions:

blocks.caption: P is the set of non-padding token positions in the batch; h_t is the last-layer hidden state at position t. Only direction counts, not length: a student state twice as long as the teacher's but pointing the same way costs nothing.

blocks.md: Feature losses need alignment that output losses do not: a projection or regressor when widths differ (FitNets, TinyBERT's W_h), a layer mapping when depths differ, and the same spatial grid or the same token positions. Output distillation needs none of this, only the same set of classes or the same vocabulary.

Hints match a teacher layer through a learned regressor; attention transfer sums channels away so widths need not match; TinyBERT matches attention matrices and hidden states layer by layer through a mapping g(m); DistilBERT aligns last-layer directions with a cosine loss.

blocks.question: Your teacher's chosen layer has 64 channels on a 14 by 14 grid; the student's has 24 channels on the same grid. Which loss can compare them without any new trainable weights?
options: A FitNets hint loss, because the regressor is optional
TinyBERT's hidden-state loss MSE(H_S W_h, H_T)
Attention transfer: sum squared activations over channels, normalize, compare
Plain mean squared error between the two activation tensors
blocks.explain: Summing squared activations over channels gives a 14 by 14 map for both networks, whatever their channel counts. A FitNets hint needs the regressor r (here 24 to 64 channels), TinyBERT's hidden loss needs the learned W_h, and plain MSE is undefined for tensors of different shapes.

blocks.question: A 6-layer student must learn from a 24-layer teacher with TinyBERT-style layer losses. Following the paper's uniform strategy g(m) = 4m here, which teacher layer does student layer 5 learn from, and what else is needed if the student is narrower?
options: Layer 20; a learned matrix W_h that maps student hidden states to the teacher's width
Layer 5; nothing else
Layer 24; a softmax over the attention matrices
Layer 20; nothing else, since attention matrices always have the same shape
blocks.explain: With 24 teacher layers and 6 student layers the uniform mapping is every fourth layer, so student layer 5 learns from teacher layer 20. The attention matrices are sequence length by sequence length, so they can match if the head counts do, but hidden states of different widths need the learned projection W_h.

lessons.title: Distilling language models: word-level and sequence-level

blocks.md: A language model is a classifier over its vocabulary at every position. So the classic recipe applies token by token: at each position of a training sequence, match the student's next-token distribution to the teacher's. Kim and Rush (2016) call this **word-level distillation**: the loss is the soft cross-entropy summed over positions. It needs the teacher's full probabilities (white-box access) and the same vocabulary for teacher and student.

blocks.title: Word-level targets for the sentence "the cat sat"

scenes.caption: Ordinary training: at each position the target is one-hot on the actual next word.

Word-level distillation: each row becomes the teacher's next-token distribution (illustrative numbers). After the, the teacher says cat 0.61 but dog 0.30, a plausible alternative the one-hot target hides.
The positions still come from a fixed sequence that someone else wrote. That will matter in the next lesson.

blocks.md:
A worked example on this sentence. Give the student its own rows: at the first position it says the 0.40, a 0.40, cat 0.10, dog 0.05, sat 0.05; after *the* it says the 0.05, a 0.05, cat 0.35, dog 0.45, sat 0.10, preferring the wrong word; after *the cat* it says the 0.05, a 0.05, cat 0.10, dog 0.10, sat 0.70. The word-level KD loss is the soft cross-entropy $-\sum_k q_T(k) \ln p_S(k)$ at each position, summed: $1.020 + 1.108 + 0.664 = 2.792$ nats, or 0.376 nats as KL after subtracting the teacher's entropy. Sequence-level KD (next) trains on the teacher's output *the cat sat* with ordinary cross-entropy: $0.916 + 1.050 + 0.357 = 2.323$ nats.

The gradients differ more than the totals. At the second position, word-level KD pushes the student's dog logit down by $0.45 - 0.30 = 0.15$, because the teacher also finds dog plausible. A one-hot target on cat pushes it down by the full 0.45.

blocks.title: "the cat sat": word-level vs sequence-level loss per position

scenes.caption: The teacher's top token at each position, with the teacher's and the student's probability for it. The student is least sure at position 2, where it prefers dog.
Word-level KD: soft cross-entropy against the teacher's whole row at each position. Total 2.792 nats; it also charges the student for every other word it misjudges.
Seq-KD: plain cross-entropy on the teacher's output tokens, -ln 0.40, -ln 0.35, -ln 0.70. Total 2.323 nats. Only the chosen token counts; the teacher's view of dog is gone.

blocks.md:
Kim and Rush also proposed **sequence-level distillation (Seq-KD)**. Ideally the student would match the teacher's distribution over whole output sequences: a cross-entropy summed over every possible output sequence $t$, weighted by the teacher's probability $q(t \mid s)$ of producing it for the source sentence $s$. That sum has one term per sequence, and there are exponentially many: with our 5-word vocabulary and 3 positions already $5^3 = 125$, with a 32,000-token vocabulary and 20 positions about $10^{90}$.

Kim and Rush replace the teacher's distribution with a point mass on its **mode**, its single most likely sequence. Finding the exact mode is also intractable, so they approximate it with the teacher's beam search (decoding that keeps the few highest-scoring partial outputs at each step), and the loss collapses to ordinary cross-entropy on that one output $\hat{y}$:

blocks.tex: \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SEQ\text{-}KD}} = -\sum_{t \in \mathcal{T}} q(t \mid s) \log p(t \mid s) \;\approx\; -\log p(t = \hat{y} \mid s)
blocks.caption: Kim and Rush, Section 3.2. T is the set of all possible output sequences, q the teacher, p the student, y-hat the teacher's beam-search output.

blocks.md: So the recipe is: run the teacher's beam search on every training input and train the student with ordinary cross-entropy on the teacher's outputs instead of the human references. One sequence standing in for an exponentially large distribution looks crude; Kim and Rush measured that the teacher's greedy output carries on average only 1.3% of its probability mass for German to English. They note that sampling several outputs from the teacher would be the Monte Carlo alternative, but found the approximate mode worked well. Seq-KD needs only the teacher's text, not its probabilities, which is the same shape as the common practice of fine-tuning a small model on text written by a larger one.

Three terms for the results that follow. Translation quality is measured in **BLEU** (BiLingual Evaluation Understudy), a 0 to 100 score of how many n-grams (runs of n consecutive words) of the output also appear in reference translations. **Greedy decoding** picks the single most likely next token at each step, the cheapest way to generate, the same as beam search with a beam of one. Models are described as layers by hidden units: the student is a 2x500 **LSTM** (long short-term memory network, a recurrent network that reads a sentence one token at a time while carrying a memory cell), meaning 2 layers of 500 units, and the teacher is 4x1000.

blocks.title: Kim and Rush, English to German, greedy decoding BLEU

scenes.caption: The 84M-parameter 2x500 LSTM student trained on references scores 14.7 BLEU with greedy decoding; the 221M teacher scores 17.7.
Word-level distillation adds 0.7 BLEU (15.4).

Sequence-level distillation adds 4.2 (18.9), beating the teacher's own greedy output. The paper reports the Seq-KD student puts 16.9% of its mass on its greedy output versus 0.9% for the baseline: it models only the teacher's mode.

blocks.md: Distillation is now a standard step in building small LLMs. The Gemma 2 report, from Google's family of open-weight models (2024), trains its 2B and 9B models (2 and 9 billion parameters) with knowledge distillation instead of plain next-token prediction, minimizing the cross-entropy between teacher and student next-token probabilities, on more than 50 times the compute-optimal number of tokens. Compute-optimal is the training length that scaling-law studies say gives the best model for a fixed compute budget; going far past it costs extra training compute but buys a stronger small model. In an **ablation**, an experiment that changes one ingredient and keeps everything else fixed, a 2B model trained on 500B tokens scored 60.3 on average over three benchmarks from scratch versus 67.7 when distilled from a 7B teacher. Its post-training (the stage after pretraining that turns the model into an instruction-following assistant) also runs distillation from the teacher on the student's own distribution, citing GKD and MiniLLM, the methods of the next lesson.

Word-level KD matches the teacher's full next-token distribution at every position of a fixed sequence and needs its probabilities. Seq-KD trains on the teacher's own output text with plain cross-entropy and needs only text. Both train on prefixes the student did not write.

blocks.question: You can call a strong model only through a text API that returns completions, not probabilities. Which method can you still use?
options: Word-level distillation with soft targets
Sequence-level distillation: train the student with cross-entropy on the teacher's generated outputs
On-policy GKD with forward KL
Logit matching at high temperature
blocks.explain: Seq-KD only needs the teacher's output sequences. Word-level KD, logit matching and GKD all need the teacher's token-level probabilities (white-box access) on the relevant prefixes.

blocks.question: After "the", the teacher gives cat 0.61 and dog 0.30; the student gives cat 0.35 and dog 0.45. How hard does each method push the student's dog logit down (the gradient on that logit)?
options: Both by 0.45, since cat is the teacher's top word in both cases
Word-level KD by 0.45; Seq-KD by 0.15
Word-level KD by 0.15; Seq-KD by 0.45
Word-level KD not at all; Seq-KD by 0.45
blocks.explain: The gradient of a cross-entropy on a logit is the student's probability minus the target. Word-level KD's target for dog is the teacher's 0.30, so 0.45 - 0.30 = 0.15. Seq-KD's target is one-hot on cat, so dog's target is 0 and the push is the full 0.45.

lessons.title: On-policy distillation in code: student samples, teacher scores

blocks.md: Word-level and sequence-level distillation share a weakness. During training the student always conditions on prefixes written by someone else (the reference or the teacher). At inference it conditions on **its own** previous tokens, and once it makes a mistake it is in territory it never trained on, so errors compound. Agarwal et al. (2023) call this train-inference distribution mismatch and borrow the fix from **imitation learning**, where a learner is trained to copy an expert's actions and suffers the same compounding errors. There the cure is to let the learner act, collect the situations it actually reaches, and have the expert label what it should have done in them. For distillation: train on the student's own outputs, scored by the teacher. In reinforcement learning (RL) terms the model that picks the next token is the **policy**, so training on samples from the current student is **on-policy**. Agarwal et al. call their method **generalized knowledge distillation (GKD)**.

blocks.title: One step of on-policy distillation (GKD)

scenes.caption: Sample a batch of prompts x. With probability lambda the step is on-policy; otherwise it uses a fixed dataset of sequences.
The student generates its own continuation y, mistakes included. No gradient flows through this sampling step.
The teacher scores the student's sequence: at every position it returns its full next-token distribution given the student's prefix.
Minimize a divergence between teacher and student token distributions on those prefixes and update the student. The teacher gives feedback exactly where the student actually goes.

blocks.caption: Generalized KD (Agarwal et al.). D averages a token-level divergence over the sequence; lambda is the fraction of student-generated sequences. Lambda = 0 with forward KL is ordinary supervised KD.

blocks.md: In words: with weight $1 - \lambda$, average the divergence over fixed input and output pairs from a dataset; with weight $\lambda$, average it over outputs the student samples itself for each input. In the formula, E is an expected value, which here simply means an average, and its subscript says what is averaged over: prompts from the prompt set, and outputs sampled from the student.

Why does reverse KL in particular push you to sample from the student? Write it over whole sequences: $\mathrm{KL}(p_S \| p_T) = \sum_y p_S(y|x) \ln \frac{p_S(y|x)}{p_T(y|x)}$. The weights in this sum are the **student's** probabilities, and like the sequence-level sum in the previous lesson it has exponentially many terms. The only practical estimate is an average over sequences sampled from the student. Because the log of a sequence probability is a sum of per-token log-probabilities, each sample splits into per-token terms:

blocks.tex: \mathrm{KL}(p_S \| p_T) = \mathbb{E}_{y \sim p_S(\cdot|x)} \sum_{t=1}^{|y|} \Big[ \ln p_S(y_t \mid y_{<t}, x) - \ln p_T(y_t \mid y_{<t}, x) \Big]
blocks.caption: Sequence-level reverse KL as an average over the student's own samples. Each bracket is the per-token log-ratio on a token the student actually chose.

blocks.md: There is a second consequence. The samples themselves depend on the student's weights, so the exact gradient has a term for how changing the weights changes *which* sequences get sampled. MiniLLM keeps that term and derives it with the **policy gradient theorem** from reinforcement learning (the standard way to differentiate an average taken over samples the model itself draws): each token's log-probability gradient is weighted by $R_t - 1$, where $R_t$ adds up the log-ratios $\ln(p_T/p_S)$ from token $t$ to the end, so an early token is credited for how good the rest of its sequence turned out. GKD and the Thinking Machines recipe below drop that term: they **do not backpropagate through the sampling** and only push each token's distribution toward the teacher's at the prefix the student actually produced. GKD's authors note this keeps training stable and computationally efficient; the price is that the student is not directly rewarded for steering into prefixes where the teacher will be happier later.

The second design choice is the divergence $D$. Ordinary distillation minimizes **forward KL**, $\mathrm{KL}(p_T \| p_S)$, which heavily penalizes the student for giving low probability anywhere the teacher gives mass: it is **mode-covering**. You can read this off the formula: forward KL averages $\ln(p_T / p_S)$ under the teacher, so a word the teacher gives 46% but the student only 0.1% adds $0.46 \ln 460 \approx 2.8$ nats. **Reverse KL**, $\mathrm{KL}(p_S \| p_T)$, penalizes the student for putting mass where the teacher has little: it is **mode-seeking**. Here the average is under the student, so a word the student gives zero probability adds nothing, however much the teacher likes it. When the student is too small to copy the teacher, these give very different students.

blocks.title: Forward vs reverse KL with a student too simple to copy the teacher

scenes.caption: Teacher's next-token distribution after "a cup of": two good answers, tea and coffee at 46% each, four poor ones at 2%.
Simplified toy: the student can only make one smooth bump over this word order. Best fit under forward KL (grid search) spreads out to cover both modes and puts 65% of its mass on the poor words.
Best fit under reverse KL commits to one mode: 92% on tea, 8% on its neighbors, none on coffee. Less diverse, but its samples are almost always good.

blocks.md: MiniLLM (Gu et al., 2023) argues for reverse KL in generative LLMs so the student does not overestimate low-probability regions of the teacher, and optimizes it with on-policy samples plus three stabilizers: single-step decomposition (to cut gradient variance), teacher-mixed sampling (mixing the teacher into the sampling distribution, against degenerate outputs the teacher happens to score well) and length normalization (against a bias toward short answers). GKD instead uses a generalized Jensen-Shannon divergence $\mathrm{JSD}(\beta)$. It first blends the two distributions into a mixture $M = \beta p_T + (1-\beta) p_S$, then adds $\beta$ times the KL from the teacher to $M$ and $1 - \beta$ times the KL from the student to $M$. Because $M$ is never zero where either distribution has mass, it stays finite, unlike plain KL. Agarwal et al. cite the limit $\mathrm{JSD}(\beta)/\beta \to \mathrm{KL}(p_T \| p_S)$ as $\beta \to 0$, so it behaves like forward KL near 0 and, by symmetry, like reverse KL near 1. The best choice was task-dependent.

blocks.title: JSD(beta) on the "a cup of" toy: which student does it prefer?

scenes.caption: beta = 0.1: JSD is 0.066 for the spread-out student and 0.129 for the tea-only one, so it prefers covering both modes, like forward KL. Check: JSD/beta at beta = 0.01 is 0.728, close to the forward KL of 0.736.
beta = 0.5, the symmetric Jensen-Shannon divergence: 0.197 vs 0.216, a weak preference for the spread student.
beta = 0.9: now 0.086 vs 0.064, so it prefers the student that commits to tea, like reverse KL. JSD/(1 - beta) at beta = 0.99 is 0.688 for that student, close to its reverse KL of 0.693.

blocks.md: Here is one on-policy step in code, the recipe Thinking Machines describe (Lu, 2025). Sample a completion from the student with no gradient. Run the teacher on the same prompt and the same tokens to get its log-probability for each sampled token. The per-token reverse KL estimate is $\ln p_S - \ln p_T$ on that token, and its negative is the token's **advantage**, the reinforcement-learning word for how much better than expected an action was. Then take an ordinary policy-gradient step: raise the log-probability of tokens with positive advantage, lower it for negative ones. Their discount factor is zero, so each token is scored only by its own log-ratio.

blocks.title: One on-policy step on a 5-token answer
blocks.code:
prompt = "What is 2 + 3?"
with torch.no_grad():
    y = student.sample(prompt)            # no gradient through sampling
    lp_t = teacher.logprobs(prompt, y)    # teacher scores the same tokens
lp_s = student.logprobs(prompt, y)        # with gradient
rkl = lp_s - lp_t                         # per-token reverse KL estimate
adv = -rkl.detach()                       # advantage per token
loss = -(adv * lp_s).mean()               # policy-gradient loss
loss.backward(); opt.step()

scenes.caption: The student samples its own answer. It makes a mistake on the fourth token. No gradient flows through this sampling.
The frozen teacher scores exactly those tokens. It agrees with everything except "6", to which it gives probability 0.01.
The student's own log-probabilities for the same tokens (0.80, 0.60, 0.90, 0.40, 0.95), this time with gradient.
Per-token log-ratio. Near zero where the two agree; 3.69 on "6", where the student is 40 times more confident than the teacher. Their sum, 3.99, is this sample's estimate of the sequence reverse KL.
The advantage is the negative log-ratio, detached. The update lowers "6" hard and nudges "is" up slightly (the teacher liked it more than the student did).
scenes.output: the dense signal points at the exact token that went wrong

blocks.code:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
torch.manual_seed(0)
V = 6                                    # tiny vocabulary
s_logits = torch.randn(V, requires_grad=True)   # student at one prefix
t_logits = torch.randn(V)                        # frozen teacher, same prefix
log_s = F.log_softmax(s_logits, -1)
log_t = F.log_softmax(t_logits, -1)

# (a) exact per-token reverse KL, summed over the vocabulary (GKD style)
exact = (log_s.exp() * (log_s - log_t)).sum()

# (b) one-sample estimate on tokens the student actually sampled
x = torch.multinomial(log_s.exp().detach(), 200_000, replacement=True)
est = (log_s[x] - log_t[x]).mean()
print(f"exact reverse KL {exact.item():.4f}  sampled estimate {est.item():.4f}")

# (c) the training signal: advantage = -(log p_S - log p_T), no gradient
#     through sampling; REINFORCE-style loss on the sampled tokens
adv = -(log_s[x] - log_t[x]).detach()
loss = -(adv * log_s[x]).mean()
g_pg, = torch.autograd.grad(loss, s_logits, retain_graph=True)
g_kl, = torch.autograd.grad(exact, s_logits)
print("grad via samples", [round(v, 3) for v in g_pg.tolist()])
print("grad of exact KL", [round(v, 3) for v in g_kl.tolist()])
blocks.caption: Checking the estimator at one prefix with a 6-token vocabulary, run on CPU. Real output: exact reverse KL 0.5335, sampled estimate 0.5334; grad via samples [0.264, -0.172, -0.031, 0.062, -0.051, -0.071], grad of exact KL [0.263, -0.173, -0.031, 0.062, -0.051, -0.071].

blocks.md:
The check shows that the advantage-weighted loss on sampled tokens has the same gradient as the exact per-token reverse KL. You do not have to write this loop yourself. Hugging Face's TRL library (Transformer Reinforcement Learning, for fine-tuning language models) ships a GKD trainer, now under `trl.experimental.gkd`, whose documented knobs map onto the formula: `lmbda` is the student data fraction $\lambda$, `beta` is the JSD interpolation ($0$ gives forward KL, $1$ reverse KL), `seq_kd` switches on sequence-level KD on teacher outputs, and `max_new_tokens` caps the student's samples. Like GKD's authors, start from a student that has already been fine-tuned with supervision, so its samples are good enough for the teacher's feedback to be useful.

The method has become a standard post-training tool. The Qwen3 report distills its small models in two phases, first off-policy on teacher outputs, then on-policy by aligning the student's logits with a larger teacher's (Qwen3-32B or Qwen3-235B-A22B) on the student's own responses.

blocks.title: Qwen3-8B: RL versus on-policy distillation (Table 21)

scenes.caption: AIME'24 (competition math). From the same off-policy distilled 8B checkpoint at 55.0, RL reaches 67.6 using 17,920 GPU hours; on-policy distillation reaches 74.4 using 1,800.
AIME'25: 42.8, then 55.5 with RL and 65.5 with on-policy distillation, again at about one tenth of RL's GPU hours.

blocks.md: Thinking Machines report the same shape in their own replication: starting from a Qwen3-8B-Base model fine-tuned on 400k reasoning prompts with responses written by QwQ-32B (60% on AIME'24), then distilled on-policy from Qwen3-32B,, on-policy distillation reached 70% in about 150 steps, which they estimate as 9 to 30 times cheaper than getting there with more supervised fine-tuning. Their explanation is the density of the signal: RL teaches a roughly fixed number of bits per episode, however long it is, while on-policy distillation grades every token.

For language models, decide two things: what sequences you train on (references, teacher outputs, or the student's own samples) and which divergence you minimize (forward KL covers all modes, reverse KL picks one). On-policy training fixes the train-inference mismatch, and per-token reverse KL turns the teacher into a dense, per-token reward.

blocks.question: A student fine-tuned on teacher-written answers does well on short replies but drifts into nonsense on long ones, while the teacher stays on track. Which change targets the cause most directly?
options: Raise the softmax temperature to 10
Switch from KL divergence to mean squared error on probabilities
Remove the hard-label loss
Train on the student's own sampled continuations with teacher token-level feedback (on-policy distillation)
blocks.explain: The symptom is compounding error from train-inference mismatch: the student never trained on its own imperfect prefixes. On-policy distillation (GKD, MiniLLM) samples from the student and asks the teacher what it should have done at each of those prefixes.

blocks.question: In GKD and in the Thinking Machines recipe, no gradient flows through the student's sampling step. What does that choice give up?
options: The teacher's probabilities, which are no longer needed
The term that credits early tokens for steering into later prefixes the teacher prefers, which MiniLLM keeps with a policy gradient
Any dependence on the student, so training becomes ordinary supervised fine-tuning on fixed data
The ability to use reverse KL; only forward KL remains possible
blocks.explain: Sampling decides which prefixes the student visits. Ignoring its gradient means each token is pushed toward the teacher at the prefix it reached, with no credit for how that choice shaped the rest of the sequence (discount zero). MiniLLM's policy-gradient derivation keeps that long-term term at the cost of higher variance. The samples still come from the current student, so the data stays on-policy.

lessons.title: An LLM distillation pipeline: logits, tokenizers, traces, compute

blocks.md: Suppose you have a strong open-weight teacher and want a 2B-parameter student for a product. The loss is settled, but five practical questions come first: should you distill at all, what can you get from the teacher, does the student share its tokenizer, how will you store or serve the teacher's outputs, and where does the student start? The diagram puts them in order. The text starts with storage, the number that surprises people first, and ends with whether to distill at all.
