scenes.caption: First question: is distillation cheaper than training the small model on data? A scaling-law study says yes when the teacher already exists or serves many students.
What can you get from the teacher? With only generated text, you are doing sequence-level KD: fine-tune on its outputs, including its reasoning traces.
With logits, token-level KL needs the same vocabulary. If the tokenizers differ, a loss that compares sorted probabilities still transfers the shape of the distribution.
Same vocabulary: run the teacher alongside training or store its top-k log-probabilities once and reuse them for many students.
Two more levers: initialize the student by pruning the teacher instead of from scratch, then finish with on-policy distillation on the student's own samples.

blocks.md: **Storage.** Gemma 2's vocabulary has 256,128 entries, so one full next-token distribution in 32-bit floats is $256{,}128 \times 4 = 1{,}024{,}512$ bytes, about 1 MB per token position. For 10 billion positions that is about 10 petabytes. The common fix is to keep only the teacher's **top-k** entries per position: each kept entry is a token id (a 4-byte integer, since ids go past 65,535) and a log-probability (2 bytes in 16-bit floats), plus 2 bytes for the leftover tail mass. With $k = 64$ that is $64 \times 6 + 2 = 386$ bytes per position, 3.86 TB for the same 10 billion positions. Busbridge et al. make the same calculation for their 32,168-entry vocabulary: about 129 KB per token in float32, so all of C4 (the Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus of web text, about 2 trillion tokens) would take roughly 260 petabytes.

blocks.title: Storing teacher logits for 10 billion token positions

scenes.caption: Top-k storage grows linearly with k: 6 bytes per kept entry plus a 2-byte tail mass, times 10 billion positions. k = 64 is 386 bytes per position, 3.86 TB in total.
The full Gemma-sized distribution in 32-bit floats is 1.02 MB per position, about 10,245 TB (10 PB) for the same tokens: 2,654 times the k = 64 store.

blocks.md: Truncation is not free. The kept entries sum to less than 1, and you must decide what to do with the missing mass. **Renormalizing** the top k to sum to 1 tells the student that every other token is impossible, which inflates the top entries. A **tail bucket** stores the missing mass as one extra number and compares it with the student's total probability outside the kept ids, which keeps the overall confidence right but loses how the tail is spread. Busbridge et al. measured the first option: renormalized top-128 targets raised the student's validation loss by 0.11 nats compared with the full 32,168-entry distribution, and top-p truncation at 0.9 by 0.13. Mixing in ordinary next-token cross-entropy on the real data (70% distillation, 30% data) brought top-128 back to within 0.01 nats of full distillation.

blocks.title: What top-3 storage does to a teacher distribution

scenes.caption: A toy teacher over 8 tokens: 50, 20, 10, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 percent. Entropy 1.53 nats. The top 3 hold 80% of the mass.

Drop the tail and renormalize: 62.5, 25, 12.5, then zeros. Entropy falls to 0.90 nats. A student that matches the real teacher exactly still scores a KL of 0.223 against this target, so training pushes it to be overconfident.

Keep a tail bucket: store the top 3 plus one number, the missing 20%, and compare the student's total tail mass with it. The exact teacher now scores 0. Drawn here as 4% each, but only the total is known.

blocks.question: You stored each position's top-64 teacher entries and renormalized them to sum to 1. Compared with full-distribution distillation, what should you expect, and what is the cheapest mitigation Busbridge et al. found?
options: A student that is too confident on the kept tokens; mix in cross-entropy on the real next tokens
A student that is too uncertain; raise the temperature
No effect, since the dropped tokens carry almost no probability
A student whose vocabulary shrinks to 64 tokens; store the full distribution instead
blocks.explain: Renormalizing assigns zero to every token outside the top k, so the target is sharper than the teacher and even a perfect copy of the teacher is penalized (0.223 nats in the toy). In their study top-128 cost 0.11 nats, and a 0.7 distillation plus 0.3 next-token mix recovered it to within 0.01 nats.

blocks.md:
**Different tokenizers.** Token-level KL compares $p_T(v)$ and $p_S(v)$ for the same token $v$. If the teacher splits text into different pieces, there is no shared $v$ and the sequences do not even have the same length, so the loss is undefined. With text-only access you fall back to sequence-level KD, which only needs the teacher's text.

Boizard et al.'s **Universal Logit Distillation (ULD)** keeps a logit-based signal anyway. At each position it sorts the teacher's probabilities and the student's probabilities in decreasing order, pads the shorter vector with zeros to the same length, and sums the absolute differences, a closed form of a **Wasserstein distance** (the minimum cost of moving probability mass to turn one distribution into the other) under the simplifying assumption that every move costs 1. Positions are paired by index up to the shorter of the two tokenized lengths, and the loss is added to the usual cross-entropy with weight 1.5.

blocks.caption: sigma_S and sigma_T sort each distribution in decreasing order. Toy example: teacher (0.6, 0.3, 0.1) and student (0.5, 0.25, 0.15, 0.1) give 0.1 + 0.05 + 0.05 + 0.1 = 0.30. The loss matches the shape of the distribution, not which token holds each probability.

blocks.md: **Reasoning traces.** DeepSeek-R1's small models are sequence-level KD at scale. The team curated about 800,000 samples generated with DeepSeek-R1 (reasoning traces filtered by rejection sampling, plus non-reasoning data) and fine-tuned six open models from the Qwen2.5 and Llama 3.1 and 3.3 families, 1.5B to 70B parameters, for 2 to 3 epochs, with no RL afterward. **Distilling step-by-step** (Hsieh et al., 2023) shows a lighter variant: train the small model on two tasks with task prefixes, predicting the label and, separately, generating the teacher's rationale, with loss $\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{label} + \lambda \mathcal{L}_{rationale}$. The rationale is not needed at test time. Their 770M-parameter T5 model (a Google encoder-decoder Transformer) beat the 540B-parameter PaLM model prompted with a few worked examples (few-shot) on ANLI, a hard natural-language-inference benchmark, using 80% of the training data.

blocks.title: 32B models: large-scale RL vs distilling DeepSeek-R1 (Table 16)

scenes.caption: AIME 2024 pass@1 (share of problems solved by one sampled answer, averaged over samples). Over 10,000 steps of RL on the 32B base model reach 47.0. Plain fine-tuning of the same base on R1's samples reaches 72.6.
GPQA Diamond (graduate-level science questions): 54.5, 55.0 and 62.1.
LiveCodeBench (recent coding problems): 41.9, 40.2 and 57.2. The distilled model wins on every benchmark in the table.

blocks.md:
**Start from the teacher.** Minitron (Muralidharan et al., 2024) prunes a trained Nemotron-4 15B model to 8B and 4B (removing layers, attention heads, MLP neurons and embedding channels ranked by importance) and then retrains with distillation from the unpruned model. Minitron 8B used 94B training tokens, against 3.8T for the Nemotron-3 8B trained from scratch, about 40 times fewer, and scored 63.8 versus 54.7 on MMLU, a multiple-choice knowledge test. Their advice: retrain with forward KL on the logits alone unless depth is cut a lot, and prune 15B to 8B to 4B in two steps rather than one, which gave 12% better MMLU than one-shot pruning.

**Is it worth it?** Busbridge et al.'s **distillation scaling law** finds that distillation never reaches a lower loss than supervised training when both get enough data and compute. It is more efficient when the student's token budget stays under a size-dependent threshold and a teacher already exists or will serve more than one student. If you must train a teacher just to distill a single student, supervised training is generally preferable.

Before writing an LLM distillation loss: confirm a teacher exists or will be reused; use logits when you can, text (Seq-KD, traces) when you cannot; store top-k with a tail bucket or mix in data loss; switch to a sorted-probability loss across tokenizers; and consider starting the student from a pruned teacher.

blocks.question: Your teacher uses a 150k-entry tokenizer and your student a 32k one, but you do have the teacher's full logits. Which option gives a logit-level signal at all?
options: Token-level forward KL after truncating the teacher to 32k entries
Token-level reverse KL, which does not need a shared vocabulary
On-policy GKD with beta = 0.5
ULD: sort both distributions at each position, pad, and penalize the absolute differences
blocks.explain: Every KL or JSD variant compares probabilities of the same token, which needs a shared vocabulary; truncating to 32k entries does not make the ids mean the same strings. ULD compares sorted probability vectors, so it only transfers the shape of the distribution, but it works across tokenizers. Seq-KD on generated text is the other option.

blocks.question: You need one 1B model for a niche task, and no suitable teacher exists. Training a 7B teacher first would cost more than training the 1B model on your data directly. What does the distillation scaling law suggest?
options: Always distill: students beat supervised models at every compute budget
Distill, but use a teacher smaller than the student
Train the 1B model with supervised learning; distillation pays off when the teacher already exists or serves many students
Use top-k storage, which removes the teacher's training cost
blocks.explain: Busbridge et al. find that if a teacher must be trained just to distill a single student, supervised learning is generally preferable. Distillation wins when the teacher's cost is already paid or shared across many students, and when the student's token budget is below a size-dependent threshold.

lessons.title: When distillation works, when it fails, and what it costs

blocks.md:
DistilBERT (Sanh et al., 2019) is a compact case study. Its teacher is BERT-base, the 12-layer encoder pretrained by masked language modeling that lesson 5 introduced, with 110M parameters.

The student keeps BERT's architecture but halves the number of layers (removing token-type embeddings, which mark whether a token belongs to the first or second sentence of a pair, and the pooler, a final layer that turns the first token's vector into a summary of the whole input), because the authors found layer count mattered more for speed than hidden size. Since the hidden sizes match, they **initialize the student from the teacher** by taking one layer out of two.

Results are reported on GLUE (General Language Understanding Evaluation), a benchmark of nine English language-understanding tasks averaged into a macro-score, a plain average in which every task counts equally. DistilBERT was trained on the same corpus as BERT, on 8 V100 GPUs for about 90 hours.

nodes.label:
L_mlm: masked LM
loss on true tokens

scenes.caption: Initialization: the 6-layer student copies one of every two teacher layers. The ablation says random init costs 3.69 GLUE points.
L_ce: Hinton-style soft-target loss between teacher and student output distributions, same temperature for both.

L_cos: a cosine loss pulls the student's last-layer hidden states toward the teacher's direction at every non-padding token (lesson 5 writes it out). Feature distillation: internal representations, not just outputs.
L_mlm: the usual masked-language-model loss on the real tokens, the hard-label term. The final objective is a linear combination of all three.

scenes.caption: Table 4 of the paper. Dropping the soft-target loss costs 2.96 macro-score points, the hidden-state loss 1.46, the masked-LM loss only 0.31.
Initializing the student randomly instead of from teacher layers costs 3.69 points, the largest single drop. Where the student starts matters as much as what it is trained on.

blocks.md: The result: 40% fewer parameters (66M vs 110M), a GLUE dev macro-score (on the development set, the held-out split used for reporting) of 77.0 versus BERT-base's 79.5 (about 97% retained), and a CPU inference pass over the GLUE STS-B task (Semantic Textual Similarity Benchmark: rate how similar in meaning two sentences are) at batch size 1 in 410 s versus 668 s, which the paper reports as 60% faster. Its $L_{cos}$ term is the feature distillation of lesson 5, and the ablation above shows it is worth 1.46 GLUE points on top of the soft targets.

Now the failures. Intuition says a better teacher makes a better student. Cho and Hariharan (2019) found otherwise: larger, more accurate teachers often do not make better teachers, because a small student cannot mimic them (its KL to the teacher stays high even during training). Their effective fix was to **early-stop the teacher** and to stop distillation partway through training, finishing on the label loss alone, so the student can fit the training loss. They also report that a sequence of distillation steps did not fix the gap in their ImageNet test. (ImageNet and ResNets, recalled from the prerequisite course, were already used in lesson 4.) Mirzadeh et al. (2019) attack the same **capacity gap** with a **teacher assistant**: an intermediate-sized network distilled from the teacher, which then teaches the student.

blocks.title: Bridging a capacity gap with a teacher assistant

scenes.caption: Direct distillation across a big gap: the student cannot match the teacher's outputs, and Mirzadeh et al. show it can end up worse than with a smaller teacher.
Insert an intermediate network. First distill the teacher into the assistant, a smaller gap it can bridge.

Then distill the assistant into the student. Each step crosses a gap the learner can handle. Cho and Hariharan's alternative: keep one step but early-stop the teacher so its outputs are easier to mimic.

blocks.md: Two more findings sharpen what distillation actually does. Stanton et al. (2021) are the source of the fidelity and generalization split from lesson 4. They find a surprisingly large discrepancy between teacher and student predictions even when the student has enough capacity to match exactly, trace it largely to optimization difficulty, and show that closer matching does not always give better generalization. Furlanello et al. (2018) train **born-again networks**, students the same size as their teachers, which outperformed their teachers on CIFAR and language modeling. CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 are datasets of 60,000 small 32 by 32 color images in 10 or 100 classes. The result: the soft targets act as a powerful regularizer, not only as compression.

Distillation can also transfer an **inductive bias**, the built-in assumptions that decide what a model learns easily, rather than compress. DeiT (Touvron et al., 2020) trains a vision transformer on ImageNet with a convolutional network (RegNetY-16GF, 84M parameters) as teacher, because a convnet teacher gave better results than a transformer teacher, which the authors attribute to the inductive bias the student inherits. The student gets an extra **distillation token**: a learned input vector added to the image patches, like the class token whose output the classifier reads, but trained to predict the teacher's label.

In this setting **hard-label distillation**, a loss split half and half between the true label and the teacher's top-1 class, beat soft distillation, despite lesson 1's warning about top-1 targets: 83.0% versus 81.8% top-1 at 224 by 224 resolution. The teacher's hard label is computed on each augmented view, so it can change with the crop, the same consistency idea as lesson 4.

A more accurate teacher is not automatically a better teacher, and a student that improves is not necessarily copying its teacher. Measure student accuracy directly; try a smaller or early-stopped teacher, or a teacher assistant, when the gap is large.

Costs to plan for:

- **Teacher compute**: every training example needs a teacher forward pass, and on-policy methods also need student generation. Seq-KD front-loads this as a one-time generation job.
- **Storage**: about 1 MB per token position for a full Gemma-sized distribution, so run the teacher online or store top-k (lesson 8).
- **Compatibility**: token-level methods need the teacher's probabilities over the same vocabulary as the student. With only text access you are limited to sequence-level methods; lesson 8 covers a loss that works across tokenizers.
- **It stacks with other compression**: Kim and Rush pruned their distilled student further (pruning deletes the least important weights), and DistilBERT notes quantization (storing weights in fewer bits, such as 8-bit integers) is orthogonal: the two savings combine.

Distillation trades extra training compute (running a teacher) for a cheaper model to serve. It works best when the student can realistically imitate the teacher; when the gap is large, shrink it with an assistant or an easier teacher.

blocks.question: You distill a ResNet student from a ResNet-18 teacher and then from a much larger, more accurate teacher. The student does worse with the larger teacher. Which next step is supported by the research in this lesson?
options: Distill through an intermediate teacher assistant, or use an early-stopped teacher
Use an even larger teacher so the soft targets are more accurate
Drop the soft targets and train only on hard labels
Raise T to 100 so the targets become uniform
blocks.explain: This is the capacity-gap failure described by Cho and Hariharan and by Mirzadeh et al. Both an intermediate-size teacher assistant and an early-stopped (less sharp, easier to mimic) teacher are reported fixes. A larger teacher makes the gap worse.

blocks.question: A born-again network (same architecture as its teacher, trained on the teacher's soft targets plus labels) beats its teacher on CIFAR-100. What does this show?
options: The student copied the teacher's weights exactly
Teachers should always be smaller than students
Distillation's benefit is not only compression: soft targets also improve generalization
Distillation only works when fidelity is perfect
blocks.explain: No compression happened, yet the student generalized better. Combined with Stanton et al.'s finding that students often do not match their teachers closely, this shows the soft-target signal acts as a regularizer, not just as a copy mechanism.

blocks.question: DeiT computes the teacher's hard label on every augmented crop the student sees, not once per image. Which earlier idea is this, and what goes wrong without it?
options: Patience: without it the schedule is too short to fit the teacher
Consistency: a label computed once per image can describe a different crop from the one the student sees
Temperature: hard labels need the T squared factor
Capacity gap: the teacher is too large for the student
blocks.explain: DeiT notes the teacher's hard label may change with the augmentation. Computing it on the student's exact view is Beyer et al.'s consistent teaching (lesson 4); a label cached once per image is the fixed-teacher setup that overfits on long runs.
